facts.claim: NIST SP 800-38D (2007): AES-GCM must never reuse its one-time starting value (the IV) with the same key, and a check value sent with it catches any change to the ciphertext.
Whitfield Diffie and Martin Hellman published key agreement over an open line in 1976, in “New Directions in Cryptography”.
RFC 7748 (2016): X25519, Diffie–Hellman on Curve25519, uses 32-byte secrets and public numbers.
Ron Rivest, Adi Shamir and Leonard Adleman published RSA in 1978: one key encrypts and signs, the other decrypts and checks.
NIST SP 800-57 Part 1 Rev. 5 (May 2020): a 2048-bit RSA key gives 112 bits of security; 3072 bits or a 256-bit elliptic curve, 128.
FIPS 186-5 (2023) specifies ECDSA signatures, including on the P-256 curve used here.
FIPS 180-4 (2015) specifies SHA-256: any input becomes a 256-bit fingerprint, and its test value for “abc” begins ba7816bf.
RFC 8446 (2018): TLS 1.3 agrees keys by Diffie–Hellman, and the server proves its name with a certificate and a signature.
FIPS 203 (13 August 2024) standardises ML-KEM, a key agreement believed to resist quantum computers.
NIST IR 8547 (final, October 2026): because of quantum computers, NIST will phase out RSA and elliptic-curve keys of every size after 2030 and stop allowing them after 2035.
